topic: Agent Wiki Kit: Repository-Native Memory for Coding Agents
reviewed_version: AvalancheAI-labs/agent-wiki-kit @ main, HEAD commit 2026-08-13 ("launch prep: pip-installable packaging, CI, contributing guide"); no releases/tags published; not on PyPI.
summary: Agent Wiki Kit (its engine is called wikikit) is a zero-dependency, Python-stdlib-only toolkit from AvalancheAI-labs that turns a folder of frontmatter Markdown into a governed 'LLM wiki' for coding agents: it lints page contracts, links and freshness, publishes llms.txt/llms-full.txt/index.json/static HTML, and serves the wiki to any MCP client through five read tools (wiki_list_pages, wiki_read_page, wiki_read_section, wiki_search, wiki_recent). It implements the Karpathy LLM-wiki pattern - knowledge compiled once and kept current, rather than re-derived per query from raw chunks - and sits in the fast-growing 'repository-native memory' category where memory lives in the repo (knowledge/, docs/memory/, wiki/), is versioned and diffable by Git, and is reviewed like code. The honest framing for a review: the *pattern* is well-evidenced and the *category* is real and crowded, but this specific kit is extremely early - 0 stars, 2 commits, no release, no PyPI package - so the verdict is 'adopt the pattern now, watch the kit'. The decisive tension the article must handle is that compiled-wiki retrieval measurably beats raw-text RAG on answer accuracy (agentwikis.com's own blind-judged eval: 89% vs 63% correct, 7% vs 26% hallucination), while controlled studies of repository context files find NO improvement in coding-task success and ~20% higher inference cost (Gloaguen et al., ICLR 2026 MemAgents; Khatri 2026 two-agent ablation, 288 runs). The reconciliation is knowledge vs skill, plus freshness and cost as the dimensions where the wiki pattern genuinely wins.

verification.method: authenticated gh CLI (baeseokjae) + raw.githubusercontent HTTP 200; PyPI JSON API 404; no browser tools used

competitors.name: okf-memory/okf-agent-memory (OKF Agent Memory)
key_points: The category leader by traction: ~740 stars, 57 forks (gh API 2026-10-01); pure Go, MIT, zero dependencies, embedded MCP server (okf mcp).

Implements Google's Open Knowledge Format (OKF) v0.2 as repo-resident Markdown + YAML frontmatter under knowledge/, with provenance (sources), trust tiers (generated vs verified) and lifecycle metadata (status, stale_after).

Dual-Memory Agent Architecture (DMAA): a 'push' layer (normative ~100-150-token AGENTS.md codex, invariants/tone/guardrails) plus a 'pull' layer (semantic domain memory retrieved on demand) - an explicit answer to the prompt-monolith vs RAG-blindspot dilemma.
Claims sub-300us in-memory BM25 search, ~4ms graph validation, ~80% token-bloat reduction, zero embedding API cost, and a Search-Before-Write principle to stop concept duplication.
Show HN 'OKF Agent Memory' scored 81 points / 32 comments (2026-09-05); commenters asked about benchmarking against OpenAI Symphony and about coexistence with a harness's built-in memory tool.

competitors.name: esaradev/icarus-memory-infra
key_points: ~291 stars, 22 forks; MIT; an 'agent memory infrastructure' library rather than a wiki kit - provenance, rollback, lifecycle/supersession.
Three-layer model: working memory + session memory + long-term store, with explicit supersession so stale facts are retired rather than silently overwritten.
Represents the 'memory as infrastructure' pole of the category, opposite the 'memory as reviewable Markdown' pole that wikikit occupies.

competitors.name: oliver-zehentleitner/keep-the-why
key_points: ~165 stars, 9 forks; MIT; very actively maintained (pushed 2026-09-30).

Purpose-built for the 'why' layer of repo-native project memory: the reasoning behind a codebase as Markdown in the repo, versioned by Git, 'so nothing rejected is proposed twice'; no database, no daemon, no account.

Ships a lint CLI (keep-the-why-lint) and a dashboard, both on PyPI, plus a GitHub Marketplace Action and CI lint workflow - i.e. it treats memory quality as a CI gate, the same idea as wikikit's `lint` exit-1 contract.
Closest philosophical match to wikikit (Markdown-in-repo, lintable, Git-versioned), but scoped to decisions/rationale rather than a whole governed wiki.

competitors.name: JunsW/feature-track
key_points: ~108 stars, 2 forks; MIT; 'repo-native shared memory for AI coding agents' organized per feature under docs/features/<feature-id>/ with a global index.
Explicitly positions as 'memory, not ceremony' and 'current truth over stale specs'; links existing PRDs/API docs/plans rather than migrating them ('link first, migrate later').
Distributed as an agent skill (npx skills add JunsW/feature-track) targeting Claude Code, Cursor and Codex - the skill-distribution channel most of this category uses.
Ships a portable rule set (SKILL.md + references/) rather than an engine; contrasts with wikikit's deterministic engine-plus-MCP approach.

competitors.name: waittim/MemoryCustodian
key_points: ~22 stars, 2 forks; MIT; 156 commits; v0.12.0; actively maintained (pushed 2026-09-27).

Durable project memory in docs/memory/ (manifest.md, subjects.md, brief.md, decisions.md, constraints.md, do-not-use.md, inbox.md) with manifest-driven context routing and a bounded 'context pack' loaded before work.
Its whole pitch is anti-context-bloat: 'Durable memory. Minimal context.' - a direct acknowledgement that dumping everything into AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md makes every task heavier.
Has an explicitly scoped forgetting operation with honest limits (cannot guarantee erasure from Git history or distributed copies), plus a candidate-memory inbox for unconfirmed observations.

competitors.name: vanillaflava/llm-wiki-skills
key_points: ~68 stars, 8 forks; MIT; 'turn your markdown vault into a compounding knowledge wiki (Karpathy inspired)' via six agent skills.
Skill-only distribution (no engine, no MCP server) - the lightest end of the spectrum; closest to wikikit's skills/wiki-ingest/ ingredient but without the lint/build/serve machinery.

competitors.name: cobibean/agent-memory-wiki
key_points: ~23 stars, MIT; Obsidian-powered daily logs, session logs, /prepforreset handoffs and a 'wiki janitor' skill for AI agents.
Represents the Obsidian-vault-as-agent-memory school; human-in-the-loop reading is the point, not agent-only retrieval.

competitors.name: iamsashank09/llm-wiki-kit
key_points: ~61 stars; 'Stop re-explaining your research to your AI agent' - persistent, LLM-maintained wikis that compound over time.

The nearest name-collision to 'agent-wiki-kit': an unaffiliated kit using almost identical vocabulary (wiki + kit + compounding), which is a real SEO/serp-similarity consideration for the article and a caution against conflating the two projects.

competitors.name: Zekun's blog - MemoryCustodian writeup
key_points: Practitioner writeup of the docs/memory/ pattern from MemoryCustodian's author; useful secondary framing for the review's 'how these tools differ' section.

competitors.name: dgr8akki/engram
key_points: ~5 stars; 'Offline MCP memory server for AI coding tools to share memory' - the share-across-tools framing.
Low traction, but it shows the other dominant packaging choice in the category: a memory MCP server (rather than a skill), which is also wikikit's `serve` mode.

competitors.name: fellowgeek/mcp-memory
key_points: ~218 stars, 15 forks; MIT; an OKF-backed MCP server delivering persistent long-term memory with SQLite FTS5 search.
Show HN 'MCP Memory - Fast Agent Memory Using Google's OKF and SQLite FTS5' scored 70 points / 36 comments (2026-08-13).
The hybrid representative: Markdown/OKF on disk for reviewability PLUS a SQLite FTS5 index for speed - the pragmatic middle ground between wikikit's pure-stdlib search and a vector database.

competitors.name: syiibfs-hash/cc-agent-brain
key_points: ~94 stars, MIT; 'local-first memory engine for coding agents (Claude Code/Cursor/Codex): SQLite+FTS5 retrieval, versioned bi-temporal memory'.

Bi-temporal versioning (valid time vs transaction time) is the most rigorous treatment of 'what was true when' in the category - directly comparable to wikikit's much simpler last_verified + STALE lint.

competitors.name: llm-wiki.net (commercial, Show HN 16 pts)
key_points: Ships as a Claude Code plugin, a Codex plugin, an OpenCode instruction file or a portable AGENTS.md; Obsidian-compatible.

Feature-maximalist: one command spins up a topic wiki and dispatches up to ten parallel agents, thesis-driven investigation, source ingestion, wiki compilation, project knowledge checkpoints, artifact generation (reports, decks, study guides).
'Sessions every run compounds' - it sells the same compounding-wiki thesis as wikikit, but as a hosted/productized workflow rather than a 7-module stdlib engine.

competitors.name: agentwikis.com (the serving model wikikit explicitly follows)
key_points: Commercial maintained-wiki service; the README of agent-wiki-kit names its 'serving model' as the pattern it follows.

Publishes its own blind-judged eval (27 tasks on Hermes Agent, a ~2-month-old project releasing every 3-5 days, same model and token budget per condition, replicated across two model families): RAG over compiled wiki 89% correct / 7% hallucination vs RAG over raw sources 63% / 26%; web search 48% / 48%; parametric-only 4% / 85%.
Cost/latency: ~$0.0016 vs $0.0054 per query and ~1.2s vs ~3.6s (~3x cheaper and faster than live web search); 100% vs 25% on change-aware questions ('what changed in vX?').

Publishes its losses too: web search wins simple lookups on mature, exhaustively documented domains; 'wiki first, web on gaps' routing scored 93%, above either alone. Agents read wikis natively as plain Markdown with llms.txt at /llms.txt.
Explicit 'compiling is what does the work' claim: rows 3 vs 4 differ only in raw chunks vs compiled pages - 63% to 89% accuracy, 26% to 7% hallucination.

competitors.name: Karpathy - LLM Wiki (the origin pattern)
key_points: The idea file both agent-wiki-kit and most competitors cite: the LLM incrementally builds and maintains a persistent wiki between you and the raw sources; knowledge is compiled once then kept current, not re-derived per query.

'The cross-references are already there. The contradictions have already been flagged. The synthesis already reflects everything you've read.' The agent does the summarizing, cross-referencing, filing and bookkeeping; the human curates and asks questions.
Recommended workloop: agent on one side, Obsidian on the other - 'Obsidian is the IDE; the LLM is the programmer; the wiki is the codebase.'
Show HN 'LLM Wiki - example of an idea file' scored 296 points / 95 comments (2026-04-04) - the highest-signal discussion in the category.

competitors.name: nex-crm/wuphf (Show HN 260 pts)
key_points: 'A Karpathy-style LLM wiki your agents maintain (Markdown and Git)' - 260 points / 114 comments, the largest Show HN in the category.
Top comments show the two recurring reader objections the review should address head-on: 'how does markdown help in durability?' and 'why not an Obsidian vault with a plugin?'

stats.fact: AvalancheAI-labs/agent-wiki-kit was created 2026-08-13 and last pushed 2026-08-13; it has 0 stars, 0 forks, 0 open issues, 0 tags and 0 releases.
The repository contains exactly 2 commits, both on 2026-08-13: 'wikikit: one zero-dependency engine for every LLM wiki' and 'launch prep: pip-installable packaging, CI, contributing guide'.

wikikit is not published on PyPI: both https://pypi.org/pypi/wikikit/json and https://pypi.org/pypi/agent-wiki-kit/json return HTTP 404, so the README's 'pip install -e .' / 'once published' caveat is load-bearing, not provisional.

The engine is ~40 tracked files and 7 substantive Python modules, all standard library only: build.py (16.4 KB), mcp_server.py (7.9 KB), wiki.py (6.8 KB), cli.py (5.3 KB), lint.py (3.5 KB), frontmatter.py (3.3 KB), ingest.py (3.1 KB), search.py (2.3 KB).
wikikit exposes five MCP tools - wiki_list_pages, wiki_read_page, wiki_read_section, wiki_search, wiki_recent - and pages are re-read on each call, so edits are live without restarting the server.
Lint rules split into errors that exit 1 (MALFORMED, MISSING_FIELD, BAD_STATUS, BAD_DATE, UNKNOWN_TYPE, BROKEN_LINK) and warnings (STALE, ORPHAN, NO_SUMMARY) - making wiki quality CI-gateable.

The page contract is title, type (from wiki.yaml page_types), status (live|draft|deprecated|planned), last_verified (a date asserting 'checked against reality on this date'), summary, sources and tags.

agent-wiki-kit's own evidence page claims a roughly 26-30% accuracy gain for agents grounded in structured, curated knowledge vs raw-text RAG, citing WordLift 2026 and Amazon KDD 2025 - and explicitly caveats the percentage as directional, not a universal constant.

agentwikis.com's published eval (27 tasks, Hermes Agent, blind LLM judge, two model families) reports 89% correct / 7% hallucination for RAG over a compiled wiki vs 63% / 26% for RAG over raw sources, 48% / 48% for live web search and 4% / 85% for parametric-only.

The same eval reports RAG over the compiled wiki at ~$0.0016 vs $0.0054 per query and ~1.2s vs ~3.6s - roughly 3x cheaper and faster than live web search - and 100% vs 25% accuracy on change-aware questions.

The same eval's honest bound: web search still wins simple lookups on mature, exhaustively documented domains, and a 'wiki first, web on gaps' routing policy scored 93% - higher than either channel alone.

Gloaguen et al., 'Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents?' (arXiv 2602.11988, v2 rev. 2026-06-23; ICLR 2026 MemAgents oral & runner-up best paper) find context files give no task-success improvement while increasing inference cost by over 20% on average, across multiple LLMs and coding agents and for both LLM-generated and developer-committed files.

Gloaguen et al. additionally find instructions in context files are well followed, but repository overviews - popular and provider-recommended - are not helpful, and conclude human-written context files should describe only minimal non-inferable requirements.

Lulla et al., 'On the Impact of AGENTS.md Files on the Efficiency of AI Coding Agents' (arXiv 2601.20404, ICSE JAWs 2026), analyzing 10 repositories and 124 pull requests with a paired with/without design, find median wall-clock runtime falls 28.64% (98.57s to 70.34s) and median output tokens fall 16.58% (2,925 to 2,440) with AGENTS.md present, at comparable task completion (Wilcoxon signed-rank, p < 0.05).

Lulla et al. also report mean runtime -20.27%, mean output tokens -20.08%, mean input tokens -9.73% and mean cached input tokens -9.97%; medians for input/total tokens are essentially unchanged or marginally higher, so the gains concentrate in high-cost runs.

Khatri, 'Do Context Files Help Coding Agents? A Two-Agent Ablation Study on Real Repositories' (arXiv 2607.27250, 2026-07-28), runs 288 evaluated runs (17 tasks x 3 strategies x 3 repeats across Claude Code and Codex with gold-test evaluation) and finds context-injection strategy does not measurably move correctness on either agent, bounded to <=10-15 percentage points via equivalence testing.

Khatri's failure-mode triage attributes the null to agents failing on implementation skill - feature design, pattern selection, exact wiring - not missing repository knowledge; a manipulation probe found the real AGENTS.md never converted a near-miss to a pass on either agent.

Khatri's 'selective' condition - topic-organized wiki files the agent retrieves on demand via its Read tool - is the closest experimental proxy for the wiki pattern, and it produced no correctness gain over always-on or no context in that harness.

The three studies are genuinely contradictory and each side is defensible: Lulla et al. find efficiency gains, Gloaguen et al. find no task-completion effect with >20% higher cost, and Khatri attributes the disagreement partly to single-agent studies drawing tasks from different agents' informative difficulty bands (borderline-task difficulty Spearman rho = 0.75).

The 'repository-native memory' GitHub query returns only 25 repositories, versus 6,530 for 'llm-wiki', 1,004 for 'agent memory markdown' and 319 for 'wiki memory agent' - the exact-phrase niche is tiny while the surrounding category is crowded.
Karpathy's LLM Wiki idea-file gist discussion scored 296 points and 95 comments on Hacker News (2026-04-04); the Karpathy-style wuphf Show HN scored 260 points / 114 comments (2026-04-25).

AGENTS.md is described on its own site as 'used by over 60k open-source projects'; its Show HN thread scored 837 points / 382 comments (2025-08-20), and 'Claude Code now reads AGENTS.md if there is no Claude.md' scored 741 points / 285 comments (2026-09-18).

The llms.txt proposal (Jeremy Howard, published 2024-09-03, modified 2026-08-10 for v2) reports thousands of sites publishing llms.txt, documentation platforms generating one automatically, and Chrome's Lighthouse auditing sites for one as part of its agentic browsing checks; OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini publish llms.txt for their own developer docs.

okf-memory/okf-agent-memory is the category's traction leader at ~740 stars / 57 forks, MIT, Go, with a Trendshift '#2 Go Trending' badge, and implements Google OKF v0.2 with sub-300us BM25 search and ~80% claimed token-bloat reduction.

Traction is extremely uneven across the category: okf-agent-memory ~740 stars, icarus-memory-infra ~291, fellowgeek/mcp-memory ~218, keep-the-why ~165, feature-track ~108, cc-agent-brain ~94, llm-wiki-skills ~68, iamsashank09/llm-wiki-kit ~61, agent-memory-wiki ~23, MemoryCustodian ~22, engram ~5, and agent-wiki-kit itself 0.

A related Show HN, 'Agent memory as a file format' (calpaterson.com/memoryfields.html, 2026-08-31), scored 191 points / 96 comments, with skeptical top comments including 'That's a whole lot of text to say it's markdown' and 'I'm not convinced an unstructured collection of memory files is the way to go at all'.

Kage, a third-party verification/freshness layer for Google's OKF agent memory, showed on HN at only 4 points (2026) - evidence that add-on freshness tooling for this category is even earlier-stage than the kits themselves.

wikikit's `ingest` compiles a source using the `claude` CLI (or the interactive skills/wiki-ingest skill), so the deterministic engine depends on an external agent CLI for the non-deterministic compilation step - a coupling worth flagging in a review.

wikikit's roadmap lists four instance profiles built from the same engine: market/competitor wiki, key-account wiki, data-asset wiki and ops wiki (runbooks + known-error DB) - i.e. the project positions itself as a multi-domain engine, not a coding-agent-only tool.
Directories starting with an underscore (_raw, _meta, _site) are operational and never served, and [[wikilinks]] are first-class lint targets in both [[slug]] and relative .md link form.

angles: Lead with the honest verdict: Agent Wiki Kit is the most precisely engineered expression of the repo-native-wiki pattern, and it has 0 stars, 2 commits and no PyPI release - the article's value is that it reviews the pattern and its evidence properly rather than hyping an empty repo.

The kit's real bet is not retrieval but governance: a page contract (type/status/last_verified/summary/sources/tags) plus lint errors that exit 1 turns 'did the agent remember?' into a CI-checkable property - nobody else in the category ships build + lint + serve in one zero-dependency engine.

Zero dependencies is a genuine architectural choice, not a stunt: Python 3.10+ stdlib only means no lockfile rot, no transitive supply-chain surface and no embedding API bill; the cost is that search is lexical and ingest shells out to the claude CLI.

The wiki is the artifact, the engine is the contract: wikikit deliberately separates deterministic machinery (lint/build/serve) from non-deterministic compilation (the wiki-ingest skill), which is a cleaner division of labour than tools that let the model own page generation.

Compiled beats raw on answer accuracy - and the numbers are public: agentwikis.com's blind-judged eval shows 63% to 89% correct and 26% to 7% hallucination for the ONLY change being raw chunks vs compiled pages, with the same model, retrieval and token budget.

But compiled does not beat raw on coding-task success: Gloaguen et al. and Khatri's 288-run ablation both find context files (including topic-organized wiki files) do not move correctness - and Gloaguen finds >20% higher inference cost.

Reconciliation is the intellectual spine of the piece: the retrieval studies measure answer accuracy (does the agent state the right fact?) while the SE studies measure task success (does the agent write a patch that passes tests?) - Khatri's triage says agents fail on implementation skill, not missing repository knowledge, so a wiki helps knowledge-shaped questions and does nothing for skill-shaped ones.

Freshness is the one dimension with an unambiguous, mechanism-backed win: last_verified plus STALE/ORPHAN lint in the kit maps onto agentwikis.com's 100% vs 25% on change-aware questions ('what changed in vX?') and onto Kage's whole reason for existing.

The prompt-monolith problem is real and quantified: AGENTS.md adds context to every turn, and the >20% cost increase in Gloaguen et al. is the price of that monolith - which is exactly why OKF's DMAA (tiny normative push layer + on-demand pull layer) and MemoryCustodian's bounded context pack exist.

The cost story cuts both ways and the article should show the arithmetic: Lulla et al.'s -28.64% median runtime and -16.58% median output tokens is real money, but the same family of studies puts the context-file cost premium at ~20%, so the net depends entirely on whether your file short-circuits exploration or just adds noise.

The community's own objections are the best source of nuance: 'That's a whole lot of text to say it's markdown' and 'I'm not convinced an unstructured collection of memory files is the way to go' from the 191-point file-format thread, plus 'how does markdown help in durability?' and 'why not an Obsidian vault with a plugin?' from the 260-point wuphf thread.

Choosing between the leading patterns is a real decision, not a tie: feature-track (docs/features/, per-feature tracks, link-first adoption), MemoryCustodian (docs/memory/, manifest-routed context packs, candidate inbox), keep-the-why (the 'why' layer / ADRs, PyPI lint CLI + Marketplace Action), OKF Agent Memory (formal spec, Go binary, BM25, trust tiers), and wikikit (whole governed wiki, stdlib engine, llms.txt output).

Repo-native vs database is the packaging axis worth drawing explicitly: Git gives you diff, blame, revert, review and branch semantics for free on knowledge/ or docs/, whereas SQLite+FTS5 (cc-agent-brain, mcp-memory) buys speed and bi-temporal queries but reintroduces an opaque artifact.

llms.txt is the quiet distribution unlock: the kit emits llms.txt/llms-full.txt/index.json/static HTML, and llms.txt now has enough adoption (thousands of sites, Lighthouse agentic-browsing audit, AI labs publishing their own) that 'publish your wiki for agents' is a credible answer rather than a novelty.

Cross-agent portability is the strongest practical argument in 2026: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and OpenCode all read Markdown in the repo, so a repo-native wiki survives a tool switch in a way that any single vendor's memory feature does not.

Flag the naming hazard: 'agent-wiki-kit' by AvalancheAI-labs is not iamsashank09/llm-wiki-kit (~61 stars) and not llm-wiki.net (commercial) - near-identical vocabulary across three unrelated projects means searchers and readers will conflate them.

Give the reader a decision rule rather than a ranking: adopt repo-native memory now if your pain is onboarding, conventions and 'why was this rejected' (knowledge-shaped); wait if your pain is agents writing wrong patches (skill-shaped), where the evidence says a wiki will not help.

A review must grade the roadmap honestly: four instance profiles are listed as roadmap, there are no tests visible in the tree, no release, and ingest depends on an external CLI - so 'adopt the pattern, watch the kit' is the defensible verdict.

Claim 'it is a real working engine, not a README' -> 40 tracked blobs, 7 substantive modules totalling ~48 KB of Python (build.py 16.4 KB, mcp_server.py 7.9 KB, wiki.py 6.8 KB, cli.py 5.3 KB, lint.py 3.5 KB, frontmatter.py 3.3 KB, ingest.py 3.1 KB, search.py 2.3 KB), plus a CI workflow, templates and a working example wiki.

The three SE studies disagree; do not present Lulla et al.'s efficiency gains and Gloaguen et al.'s null as if one supersedes the other. Khatri's own explanation of the disagreement (task-difficulty bands, rho = 0.75) is a hypothesis, not a resolution.
